1:
The chapter opens the great debate, and the witnesses first ask why Eliphaz speaks at all, and in what spirit. The reformed John Gill observes that he took his opportunity only when Job had finished cursing his day, being no longer able to bear his friend's behaviour under affliction; very probably Eliphaz was the senior of the three, a man of the greatest authority and reverence, and so takes upon himself to speak first, or it was agreed among them that he should open the dispute. Gill notes the weight this gives him: at the close of the whole controversy the LORD singles him out and speaks to him by name. And he marks the manner. Eliphaz "answered" not because Job had addressed him, but because he took occasion from Job's afflictions and passionate expressions; and what he "said" was nothing of condolence or comfort, as the case required, but a reproach of him as a wicked and hypocritical man.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets the speech in the arc of the chapter it begins: Eliphaz accuses Job of impatience and despondence, asserts that no innocent man ever perished, and will presently relate a vision. For seven days, Clarke recalls, this man and his fellows had kept a profound silence, awed and confounded at the sight of Job's unprecedented affliction; but now, having contemplated it and heard his bitter complaint, he forgets that he came as a comforter and not as a reprover, and loses the feeling of the friend in the haughtiness of the censor. His whole aim, Clarke says, is to strip Job of his one remaining consolation, the testimony of his conscience, by insinuating that had his ways been upright he would never have been abandoned to such distress, and that a heart truly possessed of the righteousness Job claimed would not have been so suddenly cast down.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the opening more gently, hearing in Eliphaz a man who at least means well even as he prepares to wound. He comes with modesty, not undertaking the cause alone but joining his friends, and with tenderness toward one already in grief, afraid lest what is well intended should be ill resented. Yet Henry does not spare the fault the chapter will unfold: for all his fair beginning, Eliphaz will advance from a just reproof of Job's impatience to an unjust charge of hypocrisy, doing, without knowing it, the very work Satan had failed to do in heaven. The three witnesses thus set the scene together: a respected elder breaks the long silence, and the comfort Job needs is turned, almost from the first word, into a trial sharper than his boils.
2:
Six voices gather on Eliphaz's careful, almost apologetic preface. The reformed John Gill hears him speaking for all three friends, who had plainly consulted together, compared their judgments of Job, and settled a plan of attack and the order in which each should proceed; the words hover between a doubt whether to speak and a resolve to do so — shall we try to drop a word to thee, who art already grieved and bowed down under thy burden? — fearing that any speech will only make him more impatient, yet determined to venture it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the same double note of modesty and tenderness: Eliphaz will not manage the cause alone but joins his friends, "we will commune with thee"; he promises little, begging leave only to assay or attempt something pertinent, as many weighty discourses have gone modestly under the title of essays; and he is afraid of grieving one already in grief, lest he add affliction to the afflicted. Yet with this he speaks with assurance of his warrant — who can withhold himself from speaking? — a zeal Henry traces to a real, if mistaken, concern for God's honour and Job's soul.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the justification harder. Adam Clarke paraphrases: should we reason with thee ever so mildly, because we must say many things by way of reproof, thou wilt be grieved and faint, as thy bearing of thy present affliction gives us reason to expect; yet since thou hast uttered words injurious to thy Maker, who can forbear? It is our duty to rise up on God's part, though it grieve our friend. Clarke judges this a plausible beginning, and certainly far from insincere. John Wesley agrees on the modesty, Eliphaz not undertaking the cause alone and promising no more than to assay, and reads the closing clause as forced from him precisely because he hears such words from such a person as Job.

The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the Hebrew. Keil and Delitzsch note that the interrogation falls on the second of two paratactically joined clauses — wilt thou, if we speak to thee, feel it unbearable? — a construction they parallel elsewhere in the book, and they weigh whether the verb is an Aramaic spelling that would yield "if we raise," that is, utter, a word. Charles Ellicott would render the opening differently still, "Has one ever assayed?" or "Has a word ever been tried?" and sets the scene from Job 29:9-10, where Job was held in such honour that Eliphaz might well have been awed into silence; but, convinced that Job is wrong and deserves reproof, he cannot refrain. Here, Ellicott adds, Eliphaz first strikes the note all the friends will sound: that it is the wicked who suffer, and all who suffer must be wicked.
3:
The opening "behold," the reformed John Gill notes, is a word of admiration and attention at once, calling Job and every reader to weigh what follows: that this great and good man had condescended to be a teacher of many, apt and able, gifted in things natural, civil, and religious, instructing not only his own household but his neighbours and friends. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the substance of that ministry — Job had seen many in affliction and distress and given them counsel suited to their state and effectual for their relief, so that by his words and his example the desponding were encouraged and the irresolute confirmed and roused to right action, the weak hands strengthened and the feeble knees made firm.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lingers longest here, and most warmly. Job did not think it below his greatness to teach, nor did his many affairs crowd it out; he went among his neighbours, talked to them about their souls, gave good counsel, and had a wonderful dexterity in fortifying the tempted, supporting the burdened, and comforting afflicted consciences; he had, and used, the tongue of the learned, knowing how to speak a word in season to the weary. The very phrase, Henry observes, seems borrowed from Isa. 35:3-4, the strengthening of weak hands and confirming of feeble knees. But he weighs why Eliphaz recalls it, and finds several possible edges: a just commendation set as a preface to make the coming reproof more passable; a reminder that one who had comforted others might expect comfort himself; a touch of pity that Job cannot now apply to his own case the medicine he once gave others; and, as most take it, an aggravation, "physician, heal thyself," an upbraiding that borders on the charge of hypocrisy pressed in Rom. 2:21.

That colder possibility is exactly what the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears. There is, he says, a conspicuous want of feeling in Eliphaz; whatever outward signs of sympathy he had shown, he now charges Job with an inability to draw from his own principles the support he had taught others to find in them, and seems almost to rejoice, half maliciously, that one who had been so great a help is now himself in need of help — calamity touches thee, and thou art overwhelmed by it. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the rendering, tracing how the verse and its fellows run: thou hast instructed many, strengthened the weak hands, thy words have upheld the falling, the whole recital of Job's past kindness poised, as the next verse will show, to be turned against him. The witnesses agree on the fact of Job's generous ministry; they differ chiefly on whether Eliphaz recalls it in tenderness or in reproach.
4:
Here the witnesses dwell on the two images of collapse that Job's counsel had once braced. The reformed John Gill unfolds the "falling," or, as he prefers, "stumbling," in three ways. It may be the man stumbling at the providence of God, offended that good men are afflicted while the wicked prosper, the stumbling-block of God's people in every age; or the man stumbling and ready to fall away from true religion under the revilings and persecutions of the world, a danger not only for nominal professors but even for true believers, though these never so fall as to perish; or simply the man sinking under his own afflictions, his strength small. To all such, Gill says, Job had been given to speak words so seasonable, and so attended with power, that they were preserved from failing and kept their place among the people of God; and he notes that the Targum takes it of those falling into sin, whom a good man's timely word may recover.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the paired clauses as one duty of spiritual charity: Job strengthened the weak hands for work and warfare and the feeble knees for bearing up under the journey and the load, and in this he did what all should do, not only lifting up our own hands that hang down but strengthening the weak hands of others, saying to those of a fearful heart, Be strong, in the very language of Isa. 35:3-4. A good word, well and wisely spoken, Henry adds, may do more good than we are apt to think. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds a brief gloss on the "feeble knees," taking them for the weak-hearted, those fainting under their trials, the very people Job knew how to hold up.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the couplet its poised rendering — the stumbling turned to thy words, and the sinking knees thou hast strengthened — catching the picture of men on the point of going down who were steadied by what Job said. The force of the verse, as all the witnesses feel, lies in the contrast the next line will spring: the great encourager of the falling is himself now falling, and the tongue that braced so many feeble knees can no longer, in Eliphaz's telling, hold up its own owner. The praise is genuine, but it is already being sharpened into a question — why cannot the healer heal himself?
5:
The reproach that has been gathering now falls plainly. The reformed John Gill reads "it" as the same kind of trial that had come upon those Job once instructed and comforted; and now that it has reached Job himself, he faints, grows weary, sinks under the burden and bears it impatiently, the very opposite of the counsel he had given others, from which Eliphaz concludes that his friend cannot have been upright at heart but only in show. Gill notes and rejects Bolducius's rendering "God cometh unto thee," though the sense would come to much the same: that God has come to visit Job with his afflicting hand. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke frames the taunt as a demand for consistency: now it is thy turn to suffer and to give a proof of the efficacy of thy own principles, but instead thou faintest; so either thou didst once pretend to what thou hadst not, or thou art now failing to use the very truths thou didst press on others.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry catches the unfairness in both halves of the verse. Eliphaz makes too light of the affliction, "it toucheth thee," using the very word Satan had used in Job 1:11 and Job 2:5; had he felt but half of Job's anguish he would have said "it smites me, it wounds me," but of another man's suffering he makes a mere trifle, as though Job could not bear to be so much as touched. And he makes too much of Job's resentment, "thou faintest," or, as the word may run, thou art beside thyself, thou ravest, when men in deep distress ought rather to be allowed some grains of allowance, and to have the kindest construction put on what they say. To do otherwise, Henry warns, is not to do as we would be done by.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the couplet its balance — but now it cometh to thee, thou art grieved; now it toucheth thee, thou despondest — setting the "now" of Job's trial in deliberate answer to the many whom he had once raised. All the witnesses hear the same cruelty in the logic: the affliction is minimized to a touch, the sufferer's cry is magnified to raving, and from this uneven scale Eliphaz weighs out his verdict. Job's collapse is read not as the natural groan of a good man overborne, but as the exposure of a piety that was never sound. The stage is thus set for the sharper question of the next verse, whether Job's whole religion was only a fair pretence.
6:
The verse can be read two ways, and the witnesses take both. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lays the alternatives side by side: either Eliphaz means, should not thy piety be thy confidence, and the uprightness of thy ways thy hope? — should not the religion thou wast so ready to commend to others now supply a sufficient ground of hope for thyself? — or he means, is not thy reverence, thy confidence, thy hope, thy integrity all shown to be worthless, since thou faintest the moment adversity touches thee? The drift, Ellicott judges, comes to much the same either way, a challenge to the reality of what Job professed.

The reformed John Gill dwells on the first word, "thy fear," expounding the fear of God as a grace implanted in the heart, no slavish dread of punishment such as the wicked and even the devils may feel, but a reverential affection for God that hates sin, departs from evil, attends his worship, and is joined with faith, humility, and holiness. This fear Job had professed and had been reckoned to possess; and Eliphaz's sharp question is, what has now become of it, where is it, and in what does it appear? The wesleyan-arminian witnesses hear the question as an accusation of hollowness. Adam Clarke commends Coverdale's rendering, "Where is now thy fear of God, thy steadfastness, thy patience, and the perfectness of thy life?" for if these were genuine, there would be no cause for all this complaint and despair. John Wesley makes the sting explicit: we now plainly see what thy fear of God and thy hope in his mercy really were; thy present carriage discovers that it was all but talk and appearance.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry names this the second and graver charge, and refuses it outright. Eliphaz unkindly upbraids Job with his whole profession of religion, as if it had come to nothing and proved a sham — hadst thou been sincere, God would not thus have afflicted thee. This, Henry insists, was the very thing Satan aimed at: unable to prove Job a hypocrite before God, the accuser now works by his friends to make Job confess himself one. He notes the old dispute over the verse's word-order, whether "thy hope" should stand before "the uprightness of thy ways," and the harsh construction some drew from it, that all Job's devotion was mercenary, a religion held only in confidence of growing rich by it. Against all this Henry sets a steadying rule from Prov. 24:10: if a man faint in the day of adversity his strength is small, yet it does not follow that he has no strength at all, for a man's character is not to be taken from a single act.
7:
Now Eliphaz lays down the principle that will govern all his friends' arguments, and the witnesses both expound it and expose its flaw. The reformed John Gill weighs carefully what "perished" can mean: not eternal ruin, for it is at once granted that the truly innocent never so perish; and not bodily death, for the innocent plainly do die; the "innocent" here is not the sinless man, of whom there are none since the fall, but the truly gracious man, guilty of no notorious crime. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott calls this the friends' great half-truth, and Keil and Delitzsch render the two questions as indignant exclamations: who ever perished, being innocent, and where have the righteous been cut off? The saying is meant, Ellicott thinks, either to insinuate that Job is secretly sinful or, more probably and more graciously, to assure him that if he is what he was held to be, that is itself a ground of hope, since no innocent person is finally allowed to perish; and the maxim is after all true in this, that God will never fail, though he may sorely try, those who trust in him. But it cannot meet Job's case, and it breeds Job's dilemma: where is God's justice if he treats the innocent as the guilty?

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the same distinction. Take the principle of a final and eternal destruction, and it is true, none innocent perish for ever, for only the man of sin is the son of perdition, as 2 Thess. 2:3 has it; but so understood it is ill applied to Job, who has not perished at all. Take it of temporal calamity, and it is simply false: the righteous do perish, one event befalling the righteous and the wicked alike, as Eccl. 9:2 and Isa. 57:1 declare. Even before Job's day, Henry urges, the counter-instances were plain: righteous Abel perished innocent and was cut off in the beginning of his days; righteous Lot was burnt out of house and home; righteous Jacob was a Syrian ready to perish, in the phrase of Deut. 26:5.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses divide over Eliphaz's real drift. Adam Clarke reads the appeal as an invitation to Job's memory: recall, if thou canst, a single case where God abandoned an innocent man; wert thou truly righteous, would he give thee over to such affliction? John Wesley hears no such openness but a veiled indictment: "innocent" implies that Job must be guilty of some great though secret crime, whose sin has now found him out, and "cut off" foretells the sickle of divine vengeance that Wesley expects will be Job's case. So the debate stands: whether the verse offers Job a ground of hope or fastens on him a charge, and whether "perish" speaks of the endless ruin of the ungodly or of the temporal strokes that fall on righteous and wicked alike.
8:
To his appeal to memory Eliphaz now joins an appeal to his own observation, and the witnesses trace the proverb of sowing and reaping through the whole of Scripture. The reformed John Gill sees the design at once: Eliphaz means to prove from his own experience that the wicked are destroyed, and to insinuate that Job, given the ruin he lies in, must be of their number. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses unfold the figure. Adam Clarke calls it a proverbial form drawn from nature, every seed yielding its own kind, and heaps up the parallels: Solomon's "he that soweth iniquity shall reap vanity" in Prov. 22:8, Paul's law of the harvest in Gal. 6:7-8, and Hosea's "they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind," whose "ye have ploughed wickedness, ye have reaped iniquity" in Hos. 10:13 uses almost the very words of Eliphaz. The apostle's "he which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly" in 2 Cor. 9:6, and our Lord's "do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?" in Matt. 7:16, teach the same law of the harvest, and even the Greek poets knew it, Aeschylus writing that the field of iniquity produces the fruit of death; it is, Clarke says, a universal law of nature. John Wesley draws the contrast with the previous verse: as Job has never seen a righteous man cut off, so Eliphaz has seen many wicked cut off; "they that plow iniquity" are those who work wickedness by design, first preparing themselves for it and then carrying it through, as the husbandman first ploughs and then sows, and they reap the just punishment of what they have done.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the ploughers as the busy, politic sinners who take pains in sin and expect gain from it, and who shall of the flesh reap corruption, according to the same word of Gal. 6:8; or, if iniquity be taken as wrong done to others, they shall be paid in their own coin, the troublesome troubled, the spoilers spoiled, as 2 Thess. 1:6 and Isa. 33:1 warn. Those who plough, he observes, plough in hope, yet what a man sows is not the body that shall be, but God gives it a body of death, the bitter end of those things named in Rom. 6:21. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott simply confirms the network of allusion, pointing to the same harvest-law in Gal. 6:7-8 and to the strange kindred expression of Isa. 5:18, where men draw iniquity with cords. The witnesses agree that the saying itself is true and deep-rooted; the fault they do not here name, but which hangs over the verse, is Eliphaz's silent application of so general a truth to one particular sufferer.
9:
The image shifts from harvest to a scorching wind, and the witnesses read it as the swift breath of divine anger. The reformed John Gill, keeping the figure of ploughing and sowing, hears an allusion to corn blasted by the east wind or by mildew: as easily and suddenly as standing grain is withered, so the wicked and all their works perish when God, moved by his wrath against their sins, blows a blast upon their persons, their substance, and their families, and they are gone at once. It denotes, Gill says, the sudden and easy destruction of wicked men by the mere power of God, needing no long siege but only a breath, as soon and as easily done as standing corn is blasted in the field. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the same picture. Adam Clarke: as the parching east wind blasts and destroys the crop, so the wicked perish under the indignation of the Almighty. John Wesley fastens on the phrase "of his nostrils," reading it of God's anger, which in men shows itself in hot and frequent breathings of the nostrils, a secret but mighty judgment before which they are blown away like chaff before the wind.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry distinguishes the two verbs: they "perish," that is, are destroyed utterly, and are "consumed," that is, destroyed by degrees; and both by the blast and breath of God, which he takes in two senses. By his wrath, whose vessels of wrath they are, the breath that kindles Tophet in Isa. 30:33, its power beyond our knowing as Ps. 90:11 owns; and by his word, for he speaks and it is done, the Spirit in the word consuming sinners, as the man of sin is consumed with the breath of Christ's mouth in 2 Thess. 2:8. The projects the wicked take such pains in are thus defeated, Henry adds, God cutting asunder the cords of the ploughers as in Ps. 129:3-4, for saying and doing are not two things with him. Then Henry catches a cruel possibility folded into Eliphaz's imagery: perhaps, in speaking of destruction by a blast of wind, he glances at the very wind that blew down the house upon Job's children, as though they had been sinners above others, the insinuation our Lord rebuked in Luke 13:2. The witnesses agree on the sense of the verse; but Henry's suspicion exposes how a true doctrine of judgment is being bent, quietly, toward a false accusation of the man and his house.
10:
The oppressor now appears under the figure of the lion, and the witnesses divide over whom the beast represents. The reformed John Gill reports three readings: Aben Ezra takes the lion for God himself, who roars and tears the wicked in his wrath; R. Moses and R. Jonah make it one of God's instruments of judgment, the literal beasts of prey he sends among men; but Gill himself prefers, with Jarchi and Ben Gersom, to understand kings and princes, the mighty and tyrannical rulers of the earth, likened to lions of every age for their power and their cruelty. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses take this last view. Adam Clarke reads the roaring, fierce, young, and old lions as tyrannous rulers of every kind, whom the incensed justice of the Lord casts down, breaks, and destroys when they turn to oppression, scattering their whelps, their children and would-be successors, without possessions over the earth. John Wesley agrees that though such men were strong as the fiercest lions they cannot escape; the broken teeth are true even literally of captured lions, but the verse means the powerful tyrants fitly compared to lions in Ezek. 32:2, who oppress for a time and are then crushed by the power of God; and he suspects Eliphaz may secretly accuse Job, or his children, of having used their wealth and power to ruin their neighbours.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry develops the picture most fully. The Hebrew, he observes, uses several distinct names for the lion, all heaped together to set out the terrible tearing power and cruelty of proud oppressors, who roar and rend and prey on all around them and breed their young to do the same, partaking of the nature of the devil, that roaring lion. Their destruction he traces limb by limb: they shall not terrify, for the voice of their roaring is stopped; they shall not tear, for the teeth of the young lions are broken, as in Ps. 3:7; they shall not enrich themselves, for even the old lion is famished; and they shall not leave a succession, for the whelps are scattered. And Henry, like Wesley, senses the personal thrust: Eliphaz may mean to glance at Job, the greatest of the men of the east, as one who had got his estate by spoil and now sees his power and family broken, a cruel turn, Henry adds, against a man whom God himself had praised.
11:
The figure of the lion continues to its end, and here the witnesses turn philologist. The reformed John Gill would render the first word "the stout" or "strong lion," the beast most able to take prey and yet perishing for want of it, not so much unable to find or seize it as unable to keep it, since it is taken from him; a picture, he says, of how God often strips cruel oppressors of what they have wrung from others and brings them to starving. He notes that the Septuagint here reads "the ant-lion," which some describe as a small creature troublesome to ants, that lurks in the dust and kills them as they carry their corn, at once a lion to the ants and an ant to other beasts; but this cannot be the lion meant, though he grants that Strabo and Aelian tell of lions in Arabia and Babylon actually called ants, that Eliphaz might have known.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets out the whole vocabulary. In these two verses, he notes, the one English word "lion" translates five different Hebrew terms, each perhaps naming a quality of the beast: aryeh, from a root "to tear off"; shachal, which as it seems to mean "black" may be the black lion of Ethiopia and India; kephir, the young lion, from a root "to cover," because he hides to surprise his prey; layish, from "to knead" or "trample"; and labi, from a root "to suckle," the lioness giving suck and then peculiarly fierce. In time, Clarke allows, these names served merely to designate the animal, much as we say lion, king of beasts, monarch of the forest, without pressing each title.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes the same observation to a different end: that no fewer than five words for the lion should stand here shows how common and how various these animals must have been in Job's country; and the sense of the couplet is that even wickedness joined with strength is equally unable to prosper; the strong lion and its whelps alike are brought to nothing, so that neither the oppressor's might nor his hope of a successor avails him. John Wesley closes the scene simply: the whelps are "scattered," gone from their dens by many ways to hunt for prey and finding none, the lairs once loud with menace now left empty. The witnesses do not divide over meaning; together they let the roaring dynasty of the oppressor die of hunger and disperse, a warning image whose edge, as before, points quietly toward Job.
12:
Eliphaz leaves reason and observation for revelation, and the witnesses first ask whether the vision is to be trusted, then how its words are chosen. The reformed John Gill defends its genuineness. Some, he reports, have thought the whole a mere fiction of Eliphaz, and some have gone so far as to call it diabolical; but there is nothing in its manner or its matter unworthy of a divine revelation, and Eliphaz, though a mistaken man in Job's case, was a good one, witness the sacrifice God afterward accepted for him, nor does Job ever charge him with inventing it. Its burden, Gill adds, is the holiness of God and the frailty and sinfulness of man, from which Eliphaz will argue that no man can be just before God, and that Job is wrong to plead his innocence.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and the wesleyan-arminian witnesses agree the message was real, but note how Eliphaz turns it. Henry thinks it would have served well to reprove Job's murmuring, had Eliphaz kept to its purport instead of pressing it to prove him a hypocrite; and he dwells on the manner of its coming, "brought secretly," by stealth, for some of the sweetest communion with God is in secret, and "a little thereof" received, since even the best receive but a little of divine knowledge in this world, as 1 Cor. 13:12 owns. Adam Clarke reads it more warily: to give himself authority Eliphaz professes a vision from God, whose doctrine he then applies in a way the revelation never intended; and, following Mr. Good, he renders the second clause "mine ear received a whisper along with it," the apparition being the general sight and the whispered words its message.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the Hebrew. "Secretly brought to me" is literally "was stolen for me," the very verb Joseph uses of himself in Gen. 40:15; and "a little," a rare word found again only in Job's own mouth in Job 26:14, means a small fragment compared with the inexhaustible store left unrevealed. He notes that Eliphaz now rises into highly poetical language, so fine that Byron rendered it among his Hebrew Melodies. John Wesley likewise reads the "word" as a message from God, stolen or brought by stealth, spoken low in the ear as God's word came to the prophets and to Samuel; Eliphaz does not pretend to have grasped it fully, but only to have perceived something, for how little a portion is heard of God.
13:
The setting of the vision draws the witnesses to the night and to the strange state in which such words come. The reformed John Gill takes Eliphaz to have been meditating on divine things, or turning over some night-vision already seen, when the revelation was made; for it is often in meditation that the Lord makes known his mind, and this was a usual way of his speaking in former times, by a vision whether of day or night. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses mark the difference between vision and dream. John Wesley explains that in dreams God imparted his mind while men slept, but in visions while they were awake; such visions came sometimes by day but most often by night, and here Eliphaz, though it was the dead of night when men are commonly in deep sleep, was not himself asleep. The very thoughts of which he speaks, Wesley adds, arose from visions he had probably seen before, God imparting his mind by such nightly showings as the church knew in the ages before the Scriptures were written. Adam Clarke, borrowing from Mr. Good, exalts the passage as beyond rival in ancient or modern poetry: the midnight solitude, the deep sleep of all around, the dreadful chill and rising of the hair over the whole body, the shivering not of the muscles only but of the very bones, the gliding approach of the spectre and the abruptness of its pause, its undefined and indescribable form; and he adds Hervey's like description of the awful being that burst upon the wakeful, solitary muser.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott grounds the scene in the language of Scripture. Revelation through visions of the night, he observes, is the manner of the book of Genesis, and afterward becomes uncommon except in Daniel; the word here rendered "thoughts" occurs again only in Job 20:2, and the "deep sleep" is like a reminiscence of the tardemah that fell on Adam and on Abram in Gen. 2:21 and Gen. 15:12, a word used again at Job 33:15 and elsewhere only at 1 Sam. 26:12, Prov. 19:15, and Isa. 29:10. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the rendering and to the flow — in thoughts from the visions of the night, when deep sleep falleth on men, fear came upon me, and trembling — carrying the reader straight from the hush of sleep into the terror that seizes the waking seer. The witnesses agree that the hour and the deep sleep are not idle scene-setting but the very conditions under which, in that early age, God was wont to break in upon the soul.
14:
Before ever a word is heard, terror seizes the seer, and the witnesses read the trembling as the fit preparation for a visit from heaven. The reformed John Gill notes that it was not dread of mind only but a trembling of the body, such as often came upon even good men at any unusual appearance of God, by a voice, by some representation, or by an angel. He gathers the instances: Abraham in the horror of great darkness at the vision of the pieces, Moses at Sinai, Daniel in his visions, Zechariah when the angel brought him word of a son. Such shaking, Gill explains, springs from the frailty and weakness of human nature, from a consciousness of guilt, from a sense of the awful majesty of God, and from an uneasy apprehension of what the appearance may portend. He does not read the terror as a guilt peculiar to Eliphaz, for the holiest of men have shaken so at the near approach of heaven; it is human weakness meeting a weight it was never made to bear unmoved.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same terror as God's way of humbling the man he means to honour. It should seem that before Eliphaz either heard or saw anything he was seized with this trembling, which shook his bones and perhaps the bed under him; a holy awe and reverence of God and his majesty being struck upon his spirit, he was thereby made ready for a divine visit. Whom God intends to exalt he first lays low; he will have us serve him with holy fear and rejoice with trembling, so that the very dread is a kind of grace, fitting the soul to receive what is about to be spoken.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the picture in their rendering — fear came upon me, and trembling, which made all my bones to shake — the shudder running through the whole frame of the man. The witnesses do not divide. Between them they show the seer unmanned before the message begins: his mind gripped with dread, his body shaking to the bones, his conscience alive to guilt and to the nearness of God. It is a terror the witnesses take to be the native response of sinful man to any near approach of heaven, so that even the friends of God have trembled at his coming; the dread is the fit gateway to the word. And it is precisely in this unstrung and awe-struck state, and not in calm command of himself, that Eliphaz is brought to hear the solemn question the vision has come to ask.
15:
At the height of the terror the apparition itself passes by, and the witnesses divide over what exactly went before Eliphaz's face. The reformed John Gill lays out the choices. Some, and the Targum with them, take the "spirit" for a wind, a stormy, blustering blast that blew strong upon him, like the wind Elijah felt at Horeb though the Lord was not in it, as 1 Kings 19:11 tells, or the whirlwind out of which God would afterward speak to Job. But Gill prefers, with Jarchi, to understand an angel, an immaterial spirit clothed for the moment in human form, passing and repassing before Eliphaz that he might take note of it, and mark that it came with a message. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees it was an angel in visible shape, otherwise Eliphaz could not have discerned it, and reads the hair of his flesh standing up as the effect of the excessive horror caused by so glorious, unusual, and terrible a presence.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott resists any crude literalism. It is vain, he argues, to reason from this passage that spiritual essences can be seen by the bodily eye; the language is highly figurative and poetical, and a spiritual manifestation can be made only to the spirit. The very notion of seeing a spirit is in itself absurd, for it would mean seeing the invisible; what is conceivable is that the perceptions of the inner spirit may become so vivid that they take on the character of an outward manifestation. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, describing the apparition, holds it to have been real and no mere dream or fancy, an image plainly before his eyes, which passed and repassed and at length stood still, yet indistinct and confused, its form not to be discerned; and its effect was a great consternation, the hair standing on end, for even the apparitions of good spirits have always made deep impressions of fear, since after man sinned every express from heaven has been terrible to him. We know little of spirits, Henry owns, nor are we capable of knowing much, nor is it fit that we should until we remove to the world of spirits ourselves; the vision was granted to awaken and inform the conscience, not to gratify curiosity. So the witnesses circle a real question — whether a wind, a visible angel, or an inward perception risen to the vividness of sight — without dissolving it; but they agree that whatever passed before Eliphaz left him bristling with dread, and that the horror of the moment is meant to lend a borrowed authority to the words that follow.
16:
The moving shape now halts to speak, and the witnesses attend to the stillness, the dim form, and the hush before the voice. The reformed John Gill pictures the spirit, which had been going to and fro, now standing still directly over against Eliphaz, as one with something to say, so preparing him to attend; it stood before him while it spoke that he might take the more notice of it. The very arrest of its motion, Gill takes to be significant: the shape that had gone to and fro now fixes in place, a sign that the moment of speech has come and that Eliphaz must give it his whole heed. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads each clause in turn: having passed by to and again, the spirit made a stand and addressed itself to speak; Eliphaz could not discern the form exactly and distinctly, but saw some visible resemblance, though confusedly; and then came the silence, the spirit, which may have made some noise in its motion, now standing still made none, all else about him was hushed, and he himself kept in his voice and breath that he might hear. Wesley notes that the Hebrew runs, "silence and a voice I heard," putting the hush first and then the voice, as though the stillness itself were part of what was to be received.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on that solemn pause. Before the message was delivered there was silence, profound silence; for when we are to speak either from God or to him it becomes us to address ourselves with a reverent stillness, setting bounds about the mount on which God comes down and not being hasty to utter anything. It was in a still, small voice, he adds, that the message was at last delivered, the manner recalling the LORD's coming to Elijah, and the indistinctness of the form was of a piece with the purpose, since Eliphaz's conscience was to be awakened and informed, not his curiosity gratified. The message was too weighty to be flung out amid noise; it waited on stillness, that the hearer's whole soul might be bent to receive it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch hold to the rendering — it stood still, but I could not discern the form thereof; an image was before mine eyes, there was silence, and I heard a voice — letting the very syntax enact the suspense. The witnesses agree that the whole scene, the halted shape, the unreadable form, the breathless quiet, is built to make the coming word weighty; all is stilled, and out of the silence a voice at last is heard.
17:
Out of the silence comes the question on which the whole speech turns, and the witnesses crowd around both its wording and its aim. The reformed John Gill doubts the common comparative rendering, "more just than God." That a poor, weak, dying, sinful man should be more righteous than the God who is essentially and infinitely just needs no vision to prove, and God would hardly send an angelic spirit in so awful and solemn a manner to declare so plain a thing; Gill therefore leans to the sense "just before God," that no man can be righteous in God's sight. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it the same way — shall poor, weak, sinful man be justified before God? shall even the strong and mighty man be pure before his Maker? — and answers that no man is holy or pure of himself, but must be justified by God's mercy through an atoning sacrifice and sanctified by his Spirit; the work is God's, not man's, so that all boasting is excluded. Yet Clarke will not let the spectre's words be stretched too far: it is false to infer that none can be justified or purified at all, when God both justifies the ungodly and sanctifies the unholy; the utterance, he says, lays bare a wound without providing the cure, and Eliphaz aims it at Job as one who spoke of his righteousness as if it were his own achievement.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry both fasten on the two Hebrew words for man. Shall enosh, mortal, miserable man, be so insolent; nay, shall geber, the strongest and most eminent, stand in competition with God? To find fault with God's law, his grace, or his providence, Wesley says, is to make oneself more just and pure than one's Maker and Owner, the author of all the justice that is in man. Henry weighs whether Eliphaz means to prove Job's afflictions a certain mark of wickedness, or only to reprove his murmuring; he inclines to the milder reading, but insists that in either case it is most impious and absurd for the clay to think itself purer than the potter who formed it.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott names this the burden on which all the friends for ever harp, perfectly orthodox and yet perfectly inadequate to Job's case. Job will freely grant that no man is just with God; but then rises his real dilemma, where God's justice is if he punishes the innocent as the guilty. The word for "mortal," Ellicott adds, means properly weak or frail man, and even the strong man cannot be purer than the Maker who is presumed to be both mighty and righteous. The witnesses agree on the doctrine and divide on its use: a true word about the creature's lowliness, made by Eliphaz into a lever against a suffering saint.
18:
The vision presses its point upward, to the angels, and the witnesses divide over which angels are meant and how to render the charge laid on them. The reformed John Gill takes the whole oracle to run on to the end of the chapter, and reads "his servants" not of the prophets, nor of righteous men in general, but, as the following contrast with dwellers in houses of clay shows, of the angels themselves, in whom God, the Maker of men and angels alike, places no such trust as creatures place in what they cannot do without. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses refer the words to the fall. Adam Clarke understands the servants and angels to be those who kept not their first estate: God put no trust in them because nothing is immutable but himself, and no intelligent being can stand in purity unless continually upheld by him; and "his angels he charged with folly" means, not that he charges the standing angels, but that he charged with folly those who fell. Clarke surveys the renderings — the Vulgate's "in his angels he found perverseness," the Syriac's "amazement," the French "he putteth light into his angels," Montanus's "exultation" — tracing them to the Hebrew word he connects with irradiation or shining, and citing Coverdale's "proud disobedience among his angels." John Wesley likewise takes the folly to refer, beyond all doubt, to the angels who wickedly fell from God, and reads "servants" as a title of eminence marking God's sovereign dominion over the angels, and much more over men.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the verse rather upon the creaturely limits of even the unfallen angels. They are God's waiting and working servants, bright and blessed beings, yet he neither needs them nor is bettered by them, and is infinitely above them; therefore he puts no trust in them as though he could not do his work without them, and charges them with folly, vanity, and imperfection in comparison with himself, not with iniquity but with a finiteness that, left to itself, might err. Some, Henry notes, draw from it that the angelic nature is so mutable that God would not trust the angels even with their own integrity, but confirmed them by his grace. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott keeps the statement general and timeless, reading "putteth" and "chargeth," not of any one past act, and observing that Eliphaz repeats himself in Job 15:15. Keil and Delitzsch settle the grammar of the coming comparison, that the particle governing the next verse means "how much more" after a positive clause, as in 2 Sam. 16:11. The witnesses thus part over whether the folly is the sin of the fallen or the frailty of all creatures, but agree that the verse humbles the highest of beings to exalt the justice of God.
19:
From the angels the argument descends to man, and the witnesses expound the "house of clay" and the crushing "before the moth." The reformed John Gill insists the house of clay is not the grave, as the Targum would have it, for the verse concerns the living, but the body in which the soul dwells, a truth, he notes, that shows the soul's superior excellency and its power to exist apart from the body in the separate state before the resurrection. The body is called a house of clay for its origin in the dust of the earth and for its frailty, brittle as clay; and he recalls that even the heathen Epictetus called the body clay elegantly wrought. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch ground the language in Scripture's own account of man's making: the clay house is his perishable body, taken from the dust as in Gen. 2:7 and doomed to return to it as in Gen. 3:19; and they weigh the phrase "before the moth," rejecting the readings that make man crushed sooner than a moth or more quickly than a moth destroys, and taking "before" in its plain sense of in the presence of.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses stress the frailty. Adam Clarke, reading with the Vulgate "how much more," argues that if even angels may be unstable, man can claim no stability who lives in an earthly tabernacle and must soon return to dust; "crushed before the moth" means that the slightest accident destroys him, for a fly, a grape-stone, or a hair can kill, and great men have died by all three. John Wesley draws the contrast with the angels: they are free spirits in celestial and everlasting mansions, but man's immortal spirit dwells in a mortal body of clay, a clog and a snare, whose very foundation is in the dust from which it came and to which it must return; the moth that crushes it is so contemptible a thing that no creature is too mean to have the body of man in its power.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the imagery into a meditation on man's meanness: the angels are pure and free spirits, but the soul of man is housed in a cottage of clay, mean and mouldering, a cage and a prison whose foundation is not on a rock but in the dust, so that it sinks by its own weight; and man is so soon crushed that he may be broken like a moth between the fingers, "crushed before the face of the moth," in the language of Hos. 5:12-14. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds only that the "houses of clay" may glance at the brick-making of Gen. 11:3, and that men are so frail that even the moth destroys them. The witnesses agree that the verse is built to abase man before God, though they render its images with differing shades.
20:
The vision turns to the swiftness and the silence of man's dying, and the witnesses draw out both. The reformed John Gill takes the dwellers in houses of clay to be always exposed to death, carrying the seeds of mortality continually at work within them; between morning and evening are numberless instances of death's power, and some men's whole life is but the space of a day, green as grass in the morning and cut down by evening. Indeed, Gill says, it is true of all men that they begin to die the day they begin to live, so that the wise man names no interval between a time to be born and a time to die in Eccl. 3:2, and our days are but a handbreadth, as Ps. 39:5 owns. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the same continual dying. Adam Clarke observes that in almost every moment some human being comes into the world and some departs; "they perish for ever" he renders as they pass by, moulder into dust, and are soon forgotten, for who now regards the past generation among the dead? And he hears the same note in Isa. 57:1, that the righteous perisheth and no man layeth it to heart. John Wesley reads "destroyed" as meaning that all the day long there is not a moment in which man is not sinking toward death, and "without any regarding it" as the strange carelessness by which so common a thing is passed over, unheeded even by the highest and greatest, as a general accident not worth remark.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the daily wasting most vividly: men are dying daily and continually wasting, destroyed from morning to evening, death still working in us like a mole digging our grave at every remove; their life is short, lasting perhaps but from morning to evening, so that their birth and death are the sunrise and sunset of the same day. The grammatical-historical witnesses keep to the plain force of the words: Keil and Delitzsch render simply that they are broken in pieces from morning to evening and perish unregarded for ever, and Charles Ellicott notes that the process is continual and unceasing, and that, when we consider the ravages of time upon whole generations, we may well say that none regardeth it. The witnesses agree that the verse's terror lies not only in death's speed but in the world's indifference to it.
21:
The vision ends on the stripping away of all that man prided himself in, and here the witnesses divide over a single Hebrew word. The reformed John Gill takes "their excellency which is in them" for the soul, the most excellent part of man, which though it does not die yet departs from the body at death, carrying with it every power and faculty, thought, affection, memory, and every endowment of wisdom, learning, and knowledge that fails when a man dies; or, reading "which is with them," for the outward wealth and honour that a man cannot carry into the grave. He notes too that a learned interpreter refers the "excellency" to the lost image of God, the original righteousness that was man's true excellency before the fall. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the line by a wholly different image: not "excellency" but the tent-cord — is not the cord of their tent in them torn away? so they die, and not in wisdom — the frail body pictured as a tent that collapses the moment its cord is plucked up.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses weigh both the excellency and the wisdom. Adam Clarke reads the excellency as personal beauty, bodily strength, eloquence, and mental gifts, all plucked up by the roots and their very memory soon perishing; and on "they die, even without wisdom" he reflects that all men die in comparative ignorance, for with all our arts we scarcely know the nature of matter or spirit, of gravitation, magnetism, or the life within our own bodies, so that the only wisdom that makes us safe for eternity is to know the true God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent. John Wesley takes the excellency for all that is by common estimation excellent in men, high birth, riches, power, and natural and civil accomplishments, which so far from saving them perish along with the houses of clay they lodged in; and "without wisdom" means without ever attaining that one wisdom for which they came into the world.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the same threads to their close. In death all man's excellency passes away, for beauty, strength, and learning cannot secure him but must die with him, and neither pomp nor wealth nor power descends after him; his wisdom cannot save him, and he dies for want of wisdom, by his own foolish management digging his grave with his own teeth. It is so common a thing, Henry adds, that no one heeds it; men have no excellency but what death takes away, and they die, unless grace prevent, for want of the wisdom that lays hold on eternal life. So Eliphaz's vision ends where he means it to leave Job: with man abased to the dust, that the justice of God may stand unquestioned.
